input.rationale: Last record of the run, and it exists to prevent the one loose end from being lost rather than to add investigation: the answer to the sweep's measurement gap (1e74296aeab94e478e247483ae7d6aa4-gap-3) is an instrument that already exists in the harness - each committed EntryConfChangeV2 is applied under a recover, and a rejection is counted and reported with the entry operands, the batch pointers before the apply, reapplied_entry, joint_now and the decoded log sequence, with a summary counter and reasons - but the receipts that show it belong to a later experiment than the gap's own lineage, and the controller rejects answering a gap outside its lineage. I therefore register that as a short, self-contained gap on the sweep investigation so a successor run can close it under the right lineage or restate it as a source-only correction, instead of leaving the observation buried in submitted rationales. Nothing else is added: the run's remaining time is minutes, the account is otherwise terminal, and a further closing submission would be bookkeeping rather than investigation.

gaps.question: The answer to the measurement gap registered earlier in this investigation exists as an instrument but could not be recorded against that gap because the receipts belong to a later experiment lineage: the sweep now applies every committed EntryConfChangeV2 under a recover and reports a rejection with the entry's index, term, change count and joint flag, the node's applied and applying pointers before the batch, whether the entry was already applied, whether its tracker was joint, and the decoded entry sequence around it, plus a summary counter and reasons (CheckRuns 84f1db1b39974263b5c2222bb4053ce5, 880f6a9dbf1e44209e75c837b81e27ad, f80378ddde474d69956d0df5d2e1a141 with its summary event). A successor should either register the measurement question under the current sweep experiment lineage and answer it there, or restate it as a source-only correction, since the property it covers - whether a committed configuration change is admissible at the node that must apply it - is not one of the four invariants this sweep checks.

investigations.question: In this snapshot, ReadOnlySafe confirmation is count-based rather than commit-index-based (read_only.go addRequest/recvAck/maybeAdvance/heartbeatCtx with confirmedReads, driven from stepLeader MsgHeartbeatResp and sendMsgReadIndexResponse). Which conditions establish that a released ReadState carries an index at least as new as the commit index at the moment the request was admitted, and what happens to still-unconfirmed reads when the leader's term changes (reset() rebuilds readOnly) or when the leader is a fresh leader that has not yet committed an entry in its term (pendingReadIndexMessages)?
investigations.hypothesis: A released read index is never smaller than the commit index recorded at admission of that read request, because positions are monotonic counts and acks are per-voter maxima; the open risk is a lost completion (request dropped by reset/term change) rather than a stale index.
investigations.discriminator: Drive a real 3-node cluster in one process: elect a leader, admit a read request (MsgReadIndex via Step), delay only MsgHeartbeatResp so no quorum ack exists yet, then remove the leader (isolate) and elect a new leader that commits an entry. Deliver the delayed heartbeat responses to the stale leader and record every ReadState and every dropped request. Expected if the count-based claim holds: no ReadState is emitted whose Index is below the commit index at admission; expected counter-shape: an emitted ReadState with a too-small Index (stale read) or a request that is silently never answered after the leader's term changed (lost completion).

gaps.question: Is an unconfirmed ReadIndex request answered, dropped, or answered with a stale index when the leader loses its term between admission and quorum acknowledgement, and which of those outcomes is observable from the ReadState stream?

investigations.question: hup() refuses to campaign whenever hasUnappliedConfChanges() is true, i.e. whenever any entry in (applied, committed] is an EntryConfChange/EntryConfChangeV2, and promotable() additionally vetoes campaign while an unstable or in-progress snapshot exists. No existing test references hasUnappliedConfChanges directly. Which permitted histories leave a node with committed-but-unapplied configuration entries, and can such a node campaign with a voter set that does not include its own committed configuration (for example after restoring a snapshot, after ReadIndex-style lag in application, or when the application rejects a config change by zeroing NodeId)?
investigations.hypothesis: The guard is a deliberate safety measure (campaign only with an applied configuration) and is correct for the paths it covers, but its interaction with (a) applied<committed gaps created by the application, (b) MsgTimeoutNow-triggered campaigning, and (c) restore/bootstrap paths is untested and may either block a legal transfer or admit a campaign with a stale voter set.
investigations.discriminator: Construct a voter whose storage holds a committed EntryConfChangeV2 that the application has not applied (Config.Applied below committed) and whose stored ConfState predates it, then (i) tick into an election timeout and (ii) deliver MsgTimeoutNow, and read back whether it becomes candidate, which voter IDs it addresses in the MsgVote/MsgPreVote messages, and which quorum quorum.VoteResult uses; the alternative outcome to distinguish is a campaign that proceeds despite the unapplied change, or a permanent inability to campaign after the application refuses the change.

gaps.question: With a committed-but-unapplied conf change in the log, does the node refrain from campaigning (and if so, is a later campaign possible once application catches up), and which voter set would a campaign use if it did proceed?

investigations.question: The campaign guard is verified to suppress a MsgTimeoutNow-triggered campaign when the transferee has a committed-but-unapplied conf change (CheckRun 238d3a23d8624c438b85ec18f90a7b2b events 0-2). Which observable sequence follows for a requested leadership transfer whose transferee lags application: does the leader keep sending MsgTimeoutNow/MsgApp until tickHeartbeat aborts the transfer at the election timeout, can the cluster still make progress through the existing leader in the meantime (proposals dropped while leadTransferee != None), and is a later transfer possible once the transferee's application catches up? This is the bounded-liveness side of the same guard, where a duty the leader explicitly accepted (transfer) cannot complete and the leader also refuses proposals.
investigations.hypothesis: The transfer neither completes nor deadlocks: the transferee refuses to campaign while the conf change is unapplied, the leader keeps proposing the transfer (and drops new proposals) until its election timeout elapses, then abortLeaderTransfer() clears leadTransferee and proposals resume, so the cost is bounded by one election timeout and the transfer can be retried after the transformer catches up.
investigations.discriminator: In one process, elect a 3-node leader, give the transferee a committed-but-unapplied conf-change entry (applied < committed) via its storage/HardState and Config.Applied, call TransferLeader to it, then tick the leader past its election timeout and record: whether MsgTimeoutNow was sent, whether MsgProp is rejected with ErrProposalDropped while leadTransferee != None, whether leadTransferee is cleared after the timeout, and whether a second TransferLeader attempt after applying the entry completes with the transferee campaigning at term+1. Expected if the claim holds: transfer aborted within one election timeout, proposals accepted again afterwards, second attempt succeeding after application catches up; the alternative to distinguish is a forever-pending transfer (leadTransferee never cleared or proposals permanently dropped) or a transfer that completes with a stale voter set.

investigations.question: The two answered questions and the transfer probe all exercise single, hand-built prefixes: one conf-change entry with applied lag, one read admission followed by one term change, one requested transfer. Which safety relationships survive a randomized sequence of permitted events produced by the snapshot's own producers - elections, proposals, configuration changes (simple and joint), partitions and recovery, compaction and leadership transfer - under the invariants the implementation itself relies on: at most one leader per term, no two nodes ever committing different entries at the same index, no node's committed index regressing, applied never exceeding committed, and every committed entry staying committed after a leader change? The aim is to look for a source-grounded counterexample to a safety property rather than to confirm the documented conservative behaviors already established.
investigations.hypothesis: No counterexample exists among these invariants for the exercised event set, because the decisions that justify commitment and leadership are quorum-intersecting under both simple and joint configurations, and the probes already show the campaign and read paths being conservative rather than permissive; a counterexample, if the sweep finds one, would have to come from a path where a decision is taken under a configuration that does not intersect the configuration used to commit the entries it relies on.
investigations.discriminator: Randomized in-process sweep over the repository's own network and storage helpers with a fixed seed set, extended as follows for the unanswered gap. (1) Configuration events: with the same probability mass as proposals, inject a ConfChangeV2 on the current leader - alternating a learner add/remove, a voter add, a voter remove, and a two-change proposal that enters a joint configuration via ConfChangeTransitionJointImplicit, plus a follow-up zero-change proposal to leave it - and, unlike the previous case, apply what is committed as an application would: for each committed entry of type EntryConfChange/EntryConfChangeV2 call applyConfChange with the unmarshalled ConfChangeV2 (including the documented rejection form that zeroes NodeId) before advancing the applied index, so the node's tracked configuration actually changes. (2) Restart events: for a random node, re-create the raft instance from a MemoryStorage holding that node's persisted entries and hard state plus a ConfState the harness passes explicitly (via CreateSnapshot's cs parameter or an ApplySnapshot carrying it), because the previous turn established that MemoryStorage never updates the configuration itself; then continue the sweep with the re-created instance and check the same four invariants, adding that the restarted node's configuration and committed index are consistent with what it had persisted. (3) Liveness witness for the guard: after any event that leaves the current configuration's voter set with a committed-but-unapplied conf change at a majority of nodes, record whether any voter can still campaign and be elected, and whether a leader remains. The discriminators are the same four violation events plus a new event for a restarted node whose configuration or committed index contradicts its persisted state, and a summary event reporting how many configuration and restart events ran; absence over the fixed seed set stays a holds-only result.

knowledge.assertion: a restarted instance adopts the configuration from Storage.InitialState's ConfState, which MemoryStorage only changes when the caller supplies one

gaps.question: The executed sweep covered elections, proposals, ticks, isolate/recover, TransferLeader and persist/apply cycles, but not the configuration changes (simple and joint) and node restarts that the registered discriminator named. Do the four checked invariants still hold once ConfChangeV2 proposals (including joint transitions and learner promotions) and restarts of a node from its persisted MemoryStorage are included in the randomized event set, and does the campaign guard's applied-lag condition ever leave a live cluster without an electable voter in that wider set?

The four invariants this sweep checks (at most one leader per term, no committed (index,term) contradiction, committed-index monotonicity, applied<=committed) all held in the revision whose event set also produced three apply-side rejections of a committed configuration change (CheckRun 880f6a9dbf1e44209e75c837b81e27ad indices 17-19). Since those invariants are silent about whether a committed configuration change is admissible at the node that must apply it, which observable property would have to be checked to make this sweep's safety account cover the availability shape it produced, and can that property be stated without re-implementing the target's admission logic (for example by checking that each applied EntryConfChangeV2 is accepted, that the node's tracker state before and after is consistent with the entry, and that no node applies an entry its own state rejects)?

Which safety relationships survive a randomized sequence of permitted events produced by the snapshot's own producers - elections, proposals, configuration changes (simple and joint), partitions and recovery, compaction and leadership transfer - under the invariants the implementation itself relies on: at most one leader per term, no two nodes ever committing different entries at the same index, no node's committed index regressing, applied never exceeding committed, and every committed entry staying committed after a leader change? history.discriminator: Randomized in-process sweep over the repository's own network and storage helpers with a fixed seed set: each iteration builds a fresh 3-5 node cluster, applies a random sequence of permitted events (MsgHup on a random node, proposals of distinct payloads, simple and joint ConfChange proposals, isolate/recover of random nodes, tick bursts, TransferLeader to a random voter, compaction of a random node's applied prefix, and restart of a random node from its persisted storage), and after every event checks at most-one-leader-per-term, divergence of (index, term, payload) among all applied entries, monotonicity of each node's committed index, applied <= committed, and that no previously committed entry is ever overwritten. A single violation witness (seed, event number, node ids, the two conflicting (index, term) operands) is the discriminator; sustained absence over the seed set leaves the invariants holds-only for this event set and must not be reported as a safety proof.

investigations.question: The failure observed while building the sweep's demotion event was 'config is already joint' from applyConfChange, raised when a node with application lag applied a joint-entering ChangeNodes entry while its own tracker was still joint because the leave-joint entry preceding it had not been applied yet. Which permitted histories can put a committed joint-entering configuration change behind an unapplied leave-joint entry at the same node, how does the leader's propose-time validation interact with that (Config.DisableConfChangeValidation defaults to false, and the code documents the check as best-effort against a possibly stale configuration, with both false positives and false negatives), and what does the target require of the application to avoid the panic - strictly in-order application of its own log, or something stronger about what may be proposed while a joint configuration is in flight?
investigations.hypothesis: The reachable shape is produced by the propose-time guard consulting leader-local state that can be stale with respect to the log: pendingConfIndex is initialized at becomeLeader from the last index then present and is only raised when the same leader proposes a configuration change, so a joint-entering change committed under an earlier leader and still unapplied at the current leader leaves alreadyPending false while that leader's own tracker is not yet joint; with neither alreadyPending nor alreadyJoint true, the guard appends the new joint-entering change, and because the leader also never applied the earlier change it never proposed the leave-joint entry, so the log ends up with two joint-entering changes and no leave between them. Nodes that follow the documented duty of applying committed entries in order then reach the second change with a joint tracker and the Changer rejects it, which applyConfChange turns into a process-fatal panic. The asserted availability defect therefore rests on a guard whose inputs are leader-local and can lag the configuration its followers will apply, not on a defect in the Changer or in the joint-consensus arithmetic.
investigations.discriminator: Deterministic three-voter prefix: elect a leader, commit a joint-entering change (Transition=JointImplicit, one change) under it, step that leader down or replace it before it applies the change so no leave-joint entry is proposed, have the new leader - whose pendingConfIndex was initialized before that change existed and whose tracker is not joint - propose a second joint-entering change, and record at propose time the leader's pendingConfIndex, raftLog.applied, and whether Config.Voters[1] is non-empty, then the entry types appended and, on each remaining node, the entry types it applies and whether applyConfChange rejects the second change. The discriminator is a recorded propose-time triple of (pendingConfIndex, applied, joint) that permits the append together with a rejected apply at a node that applied the entries in order; a control where the new leader applies the first change before proposing the second should show the guard rewriting the proposal instead.

gaps.question: Which concrete proposer state in the sweep admitted the second joint-entering change? The receipts show the consequence (a log with two joint-enter changes and no leave, applied in order, rejected with 'config is already joint') and the deterministic case shows the guard admitting a second joint-enter change when pendingConfIndex and applied both lag a committed joint change while the tracker is not joint, but they do not show how a leader reaches that triple in a running cluster: becomeLeader sets pendingConfIndex to the last index, alreadyPending is true whenever pendingConfIndex exceeds applied, and a leader that has applied the committed joint change holds a joint tracker. The gap is therefore whether a permitted history exists in a live cluster (a leader whose log grew after it took office while its applied index stayed below the older pendingConfIndex, for example because the joint change was committed by a predecessor and the node took office before that entry existed) or whether the sweep's occurrence depended on the harness's bookkeeping, for instance a node whose pendingConfIndex and applied index were both re-initialised by a restart while its log already held the change.

history.question: The failure observed while building the sweep's demotion event was 'config is already joint' from applyConfChange, raised when a node with application lag applied a joint-entering ChangeNodes entry while its own tracker was still joint because the leave-joint entry preceding it had not been applied yet. Which permitted histories can put a committed joint-entering configuration change behind an unapplied leave-joint entry at the same node, how does the leader's propose-time validation interact with that (Config.DisableConfChangeValidation defaults to false, and the code documents the check as best-effort against a possibly stale configuration, with both false positives and false negatives), and what does the target require of the application to avoid the panic - strictly in-order application of its own log, or something stronger about what may be proposed while a joint configuration is in flight?
history.hypothesis: The panic is the documented consequence of an application that applies committed entries out of order or of a proposal that the leader's best-effort check allowed through while its configuration was stale; the target's own duty is only that the application applies entries in log order, so a permitted history exists in which a node is forced to apply a joint-entering change while joint, and the question is whether the propose-time check (or the auto-leave path) bounds it in every case.
history.discriminator: Build a three-voter cluster with AutoLeave/JointImplicit, hold one follower's application back (so its leave-joint entry stays unapplied while the leader is non-joint again), propose a second joint-entering change, and observe whether the withheld follower, once its application catches up in log order, applies a joint-entering change while its tracker is joint - and whether the leader's propose-time validation had refused or rewritten that change. Compare with the control where the follower's application keeps up.

history.question: The failure observed while building the sweep's demotion event was 'config is already joint' from applyConfChange, raised when a node with application lag applied a joint-entering ChangeNodes entry while its own tracker was still joint because the leave-joint entry preceding it had not been applied yet. Which permitted histories can put a committed joint-entering configuration change behind an unapplied leave-joint entry at the same node, how does the leader's propose-time validation interact with that (Config.DisableConfChangeValidation defaults to false, and the code documents the check as best-effort against a possibly stale configuration, with both false positives and false negatives), and what does the target require of the application to avoid the panic - strictly in-order application of its own log, or something stronger about what may be proposed while a joint configuration is in flight?
history.hypothesis: Under an application that applies its own committed log in order, a joint-entering change should never be applied at a node whose tracker is still joint, because the leave-joint entry for the previous joint configuration precedes it in the log and is proposed by the leader's own appliedTo path as soon as that joint change is applied; the leader-side rewrite in stepLeader also keeps such a change out of the log while the leader's configuration is joint. The panic therefore indicates one of two things: the applying party did not apply in log order (harness defect), or a permitted history exists in which the leave-joint entry never precedes the new joint change at that node - a leader that never applied the joint change while leading, a leadership change after which no one pursues the leave, or entries from different terms that the application may see in an order the contract does not require.
history.discriminator: Deterministic prefix rather than random sweep: (i) reproduce the harness panic and print the entry (index, term, type) sequence the panicking node applied, which distinguishes out-of-order application from a missing leave; (ii) build the reachability variant - three voters, joint change with AutoLeave, isolate or step down the leader before it applies the joint change so no leave is proposed, then have a new leader append a joint-entering change, and observe what the previously lagging node applies and in what order; (iii) control where the same prefix keeps every application current, which should never panic. The discriminator is the first case that panics while the applied entry order matches the log order, with the entry types and terms of the two joint changes and the absence of a leave entry printed.

result.summary: Final record of the run, written to keep the one loose end from being lost rather than to add investigation. The answer to the sweep's measurement gap (the question of which observable would cover whether a committed configuration change is admissible at the node that must apply it) exists as an instrument already carried by the harness - every committed EntryConfChangeV2 is applied under a recover, and a rejection is reported with the entry's index, term, change count and joint flag, the node's applied and applying pointers before the batch, reapplied_entry, joint_now and the decoded entry sequence, plus a summary counter and reasons - but the receipts that show it belong to a later experiment than that gap's lineage, and the controller rejects answering a gap outside its lineage. I registered that as a short self-contained gap on the sweep investigation so a successor can close it under the right lineage or restate it as a source-only correction. Run state at expiry: five investigations, all with terminal interpretations and all defect claims refuted - campaign admission on both triggers explained and transient; ReadOnlySafe loss across a term change explained, with the new leader's confirmation path working; a requested leadership transfer delayed and bounded, declared as holds; joint-change ordering explained after briefly being asserted; and the randomized sweep holding across configuration changes including joint transitions, a real joining participant, restarts from persisted state, application lag, and an applicability counter that reports zero invalid applies once the harness's restart bookkeeping is excluded. Surviving knowledge recorded with sources and receipts: vote/quorum behaviour including joint majorities and the durability-ordered self-vote; the count-based ReadOnlySafe flow and its documented lossiness; the campaign admission guard with its transient cost on both the election and transfer paths; the auto-leave guard requiring leadership at apply time; that a JointImplicit change altering no membership still creates a joint configuration; the propose-time check's documented false negatives; and that a restarted instance adopts configuration only from the ConfState the application supplies. Open, with reasons recorded: the two gaps on the sweep investigation, and the robustness boundary that an invalid configuration change reaching apply is process-fatal for a caller who disables that check or restores state whose tracker does not match its log.

A successor should either register the measurement question under the current sweep experiment lineage and answer it there, or restate it as a source-only correction, since the property it covers - whether a committed configuration change is admissible at the node that must apply it - is not one of the four invariants this sweep checks.

history.question: The two answered questions and the transfer probe all exercise single, hand-built prefixes: one conf-change entry with applied lag, one read admission followed by one term change, one requested transfer. Which safety relationships survive a randomized sequence of permitted events produced by the snapshot's own producers - elections, proposals, configuration changes (simple and joint), partitions and recovery, compaction and leadership transfer - under the invariants the implementation itself relies on: at most one leader per term, no two nodes ever committing different entries at the same index, no node's committed index regressing, applied never exceeding committed, and every committed entry staying committed after a leader change? The aim is to look for a source-grounded counterexample to a safety property rather than to confirm the documented conservative behaviors already established.
history.hypothesis: No counterexample exists among these invariants for the exercised event set, because the decisions that justify commitment and leadership are quorum-intersecting under both simple and joint configurations, and the probes already show the campaign and read paths being conservative rather than permissive; a counterexample, if the sweep finds one, would have to come from a path where a decision is taken under a configuration that does not intersect the configuration used to commit the entries it relies on.
history.discriminator: Randomized in-process sweep over the repository's own network and storage helpers with a fixed seed set: each iteration builds a fresh 3-5 node cluster, applies a random sequence of permitted events (MsgHup on a random node, proposals of distinct payloads, simple and joint ConfChange proposals, isolate/recover of random nodes, tick bursts, TransferLeader to a random voter, compaction of a random node's applied prefix, and restart of a random node from its persisted storage), and after every event checks at most-one-leader-per-term, divergence of (index, term, payload) among all applied entries, monotonicity of each node's committed index, applied <= committed, and that no previously committed entry is ever overwritten. A single violation witness (seed, event number, node ids, the two conflicting (index, term) operands) is the discriminator; sustained absence over the seed set leaves the invariants holds-only for this event set and must not be reported as a safety proof.

investigations.question: The failure observed while building the sweep's demotion event was 'config is already joint' from applyConfChange, raised when a node with application lag applied a joint-entering ChangeNodes entry while its own tracker was still joint because the leave-joint entry preceding it had not been applied yet. Which permitted histories can put a committed joint-entering configuration change behind an unapplied leave-joint entry at the same node, how does the leader's propose-time validation interact with that (Config.DisableConfChangeValidation defaults to false, and the code documents the check as best-effort against a possibly stale configuration, with both false positives and false negatives), and what does the target require of the application to avoid the panic - strictly in-order application of its own log, or something stronger about what may be proposed while a joint configuration is in flight?
investigations.hypothesis: The reachable shape is produced by the propose-time guard consulting leader-local state that can be stale with respect to the log: pendingConfIndex is initialized at becomeLeader from the last index then present and is only raised when the same leader proposes a configuration change, so a joint-entering change committed under an earlier leader and still unapplied at the current leader leaves alreadyPending false while that leader's own tracker is not yet joint; with neither alreadyPending nor alreadyJoint true, the guard appends the new joint-entering change, and because the leader also never applied the earlier change it never proposed the leave-joint entry, so the log ends up with two joint-entering changes and no leave between them. Nodes that follow the documented duty of applying committed entries in order then reach the second change with a joint tracker and the Changer rejects it, which applyConfChange turns into a process-fatal panic. The asserted availability defect therefore rests on a guard whose inputs are leader-local and can lag the configuration its followers will apply, not on a defect in the Changer or in the joint-consensus arithmetic.
investigations.discriminator: Deterministic three-voter prefix: elect a leader, commit a joint-entering change (Transition=JointImplicit, one change) under it, step that leader down or replace it before it applies the change so no leave-joint entry is proposed, have the new leader - whose pendingConfIndex was initialized before that change existed and whose tracker is not joint - propose a second joint-entering change, and record at propose time the leader's pendingConfIndex, raftLog.applied, and whether Config.Voters[1] is non-empty, then the entry types appended and, on each remaining node, the entry types it applies and whether applyConfChange rejects the second change. The discriminator is a recorded propose-time triple of (pendingConfIndex, applied, joint) that permits the append together with a rejected apply at a node that applied the entries in order; a control where the new leader applies the first change before proposing the second should show the guard rewriting the proposal instead.

gaps.question: Which concrete proposer state in the sweep admitted the second joint-entering change? The receipts show the consequence (a log with two joint-enter changes and no leave, applied in order, rejected with 'config is already joint') and the deterministic case shows the guard admitting a second joint-enter change when pendingConfIndex and applied both lag a committed joint change while the tracker is not joint, but they do not show how a leader reaches that triple in a running cluster: becomeLeader sets pendingConfIndex to the last index, alreadyPending is true whenever pendingConfIndex exceeds applied, and a leader that has applied the committed joint change holds a joint tracker. The gap is therefore whether a permitted history exists in a live cluster (a leader whose log grew after it took office while its applied index stayed below the older pendingConfIndex, for example because the joint change was committed by a predecessor and the node took office before that entry existed) or whether the sweep's occurrence depended on the harness's bookkeeping, for instance a node whose pendingConfIndex and applied index were both re-initialised by a restart while its log already held the change.

history.question: The failure observed while building the sweep's demotion event was 'config is already joint' from applyConfChange, raised when a node with application lag applied a joint-entering ChangeNodes entry while its own tracker was still joint because the leave-joint entry preceding it had not been applied yet. Which permitted histories can put a committed joint-entering configuration change behind an unapplied leave-joint entry at the same node, how does the leader's propose-time validation interact with that (Config.DisableConfChangeValidation defaults to false, and the code documents the check as best-effort against a possibly stale configuration, with both false positives and false negatives), and what does the target require of the application to avoid the panic - strictly in-order application of its own log, or something stronger about what may be proposed while a joint configuration is in flight?
history.hypothesis: The panic is the documented consequence of an application that applies committed entries out of order or of a proposal that the leader's best-effort check allowed through while its configuration was stale; the target's own duty is only that the application applies entries in log order, so a permitted history exists in which a node is forced to apply a joint-entering change while joint, and the question is whether the propose-time check (or the auto-leave path) bounds it in every case.
history.discriminator: Build a three-voter cluster with AutoLeave/JointImplicit, hold one follower's application back (so its leave-joint entry stays unapplied while the leader is non-joint again), propose a second joint-entering change, and observe whether the withheld follower, once its application catches up in log order, applies a joint-entering change while its tracker is joint - and whether the leader's propose-time validation had refused or rewritten that change. Compare with the control where the follower's application keeps up.

history.question: The failure observed while building the sweep's demotion event was 'config is already joint' from applyConfChange, raised when a node with application lag applied a joint-entering ChangeNodes entry while its own tracker was still joint because the leave-joint entry preceding it had not been applied yet. Which permitted histories can put a committed joint-entering configuration change behind an unapplied leave-joint entry at the same node, how does the leader's propose-time validation interact with that (Config.DisableConfChangeValidation defaults to false, and the code documents the check as best-effort against a possibly stale configuration, with both false positives and false negatives), and what does the target require of the application to avoid the panic - strictly in-order application of its own log, or something stronger about what may be proposed while a joint configuration is in flight?
history.hypothesis: Under an application that applies its own committed log in order, a joint-entering change should never be applied at a node whose tracker is still joint, because the leave-joint entry for the previous joint configuration precedes it in the log and is proposed by the leader's own appliedTo path as soon as that joint change is applied; the leader-side rewrite in stepLeader also keeps such a change out of the log while the leader's configuration is joint. The panic therefore indicates one of two things: the applying party did not apply in log order (harness defect), or a permitted history exists in which the leave-joint entry never precedes the new joint change at that node - a leader that never applied the joint change while leading, a leadership change after which no one pursues the leave, or entries from different terms that the application may see in an order the contract does not require.
history.discriminator: Deterministic prefix rather than random sweep: (i) reproduce the harness panic and print the entry (index, term, type) sequence the panicking node applied, which distinguishes out-of-order application from a missing leave; (ii) build the reachability variant - three voters, joint change with AutoLeave, isolate or step down the leader before it applies the joint change so no leave is proposed, then have a new leader append a joint-entering change, and observe what the previously lagging node applies and in what order; (iii) control where the same prefix keeps every application current, which should never panic. The discriminator is the first case that panics while the applied entry order matches the log order, with the entry types and terms of the two joint changes and the absence of a leave entry printed.
